basis: Cell counts and biomass set how many cells react; per-cell rates come from maintenance power and signalling studies. Counts all enzyme turnovers (including passive reversible catalysis near k_B T ln 2 = 2.8×10⁻²¹ J); strictly irreversible ATP-hydrolysing steps in the 14 TW prokaryotic budget are bounded by ≤1.7×10³² ATP/s (at ΔG_ATP ≈ 8.3×10⁻²⁰ J, Milo & Phillips 2015).
equation: C_chem = N_prok × c_cell + N_euk × 2,000 a second, where c_cell = 10 (deep rock) × f_deep + 150 (starved) × f_starved + 5,000 (surface) × f_surface
cite: Milo, R., & Phillips, R. (2015). Cell Biology by the Numbers. Garland Science.

basis: Prokaryote abundance in soil, ocean, seafloor and deep continental crust, divided by 25 femtograms of carbon per cell (Whitman, Coleman & Wiebe 1998; Kallmeyer et al. 2012; Magnabosco et al. 2018). Past moments scale with the model's microbial carbon series; no fossil global cell count exists.
equation: N_cells = B_prok ÷ 25 fg carbon per cell
cite: Whitman, W. B., Coleman, D. C., & Wiebe, W. J. (1998). Prokaryotes: the unseen majority. PNAS, 95(12), 6578–6583.

basis: Counts of the animals that hold most neurons (nematodes, arthropods, vertebrates) and neurons and synapses per animal. Uses 0.1 signals per synapse per second as the global biosphere mean (dominated by resting cold-blooded nematodes and arthropods), whereas waking active mammal and primate benchmarks in the Atlas use ~1 Hz per synapse (~1.5×10¹⁴ signals/s for a human brain). Past moments follow the animal biomass curve and mass-extinction drops; no fossil global census of invertebrates exists.
equation: C_nerve = synapses × 0.1 signals per synapse per second
cite: Attwell, D., & Laughlin, S. B. (2001). An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain. J. Cereb. Blood Flow Metab., 21(10), 1133–1145. | Herculano-Houzel, S. (2009). The human brain in numbers. Front. Hum. Neurosci., 3, 31.

basis: Counts of nematodes, arthropods and vertebrates times neurons per individual. A count by animal group gives about 6×10²³ today: roundworms 1.3×10²³, land arthropods about 5×10²³, fish 10²², people 7×10²⁰. The census's 3.4×10²⁴ is about five times higher, mostly because it assumes 200,000 neurons per land arthropod, where mites and springtails, most of them, hold far fewer. Marine copepods and krill (~1 Gt carbon; Bar-On et al. 2018) add roughly 10²³–10²⁴ more.
equation: N_neurons = synapses ÷ 875 synapses per neuron; today checked against animal counts × neurons per animal
cite: van den Hoogen, J., et al. (2019). Soil nematode abundance and functional group composition at a global scale. Nature, 572, 194–198. | Rosenberg, Y., et al. (2023). The global biomass and number of terrestrial arthropods. Science Advances, 9(5), eabq4049. | Bar-On, Y. M., Phillips, R., & Milo, R. (2018). The biomass distribution on Earth. PNAS, 115(25), 6506–6511.

basis: Installed computing capacity and utilisation: Phister (1979) mainframe census for 1965 (2×10⁹ ops/s), Hilbert & López (2011) global general-purpose and DSP/GPU inventories for 2000–2012 (~19% mean duty cycle: 4.5×10¹⁷ in 2000, 1.8×10²⁰ in 2010, 3.5×10²⁰ in 2012), and Epoch AI / datacenter inventories for 2020–2026 (1.89×10²² executed ops/s today). Pre-1965 mechanical and relay estimates are set by hand.
equation: C_silicon = installed hardware capacity × mean duty-cycle utilisation (Phister 1979; Hilbert & López 2011; Epoch AI 2025)
cite: Hilbert, M., & López, P. (2011). The world's technological capacity to store, communicate, and compute information. Science, 332(6025), 60–65. | Phister, M. (1979). Data Processing Technology and Economics (2nd ed.). Digital Press.

basis: Accelerator inventory and utilisation for neural-network workloads.
equation: C_AI = 1.5×10⁷ AI chips (H100-class) × 10¹⁵ operations a second × 60% busy

basis: Anchored at each moment to the largest single nervous system up to 2000 CE (from nerve nets to cephalopods, fish, dinosaurs bounded by Caspar et al. 2024 reptilian scaling, sperm whales, and ~1.5×10¹⁴ signals/s for Homo sapiens); TOP500 #1 Linpack Rmax supercomputers for 2010 (Tianhe-1A, 2.57×10¹⁵), 2012 (Titan, 1.76×10¹⁶) and 2020 (Fugaku, 4.42×10¹⁷); and one 100,000-GPU frontier AI cluster in 2026 (3.0×10²⁰).
equation: C_max = the most capable single thinker: the biggest brain's signals a second, or after 2008 the largest supercomputer / AI cluster
cite: TOP500 Supercomputer Sites (2010–2024). Linpack Rmax historical #1 benchmarks (Tianhe-1A, Titan, Fugaku). | Caspar, K. R., et al. (2024). Endocranial anatomy and neuron counts in non-avian dinosaurs. The Anatomical Record, 307, 3685–3716. | Epoch AI (2025).

basis: Total DNA in living cells at two bits per letter: 3.1×10³⁰ bacteria and archaea at 3 million letters per cell (Koonin & Wolf 2008; ocean and deep-sediment cells run leaner at 1.3–2 million, Giovannoni et al. 2005) plus 9.05×10²⁸ active nucleated cells at 96 million letters per cell, sitting within one standard deviation of the Landenmark et al. (2015) global estimate (1.06±0.72×10³⁸ bits). Past cell counts follow the model's biomass series; the first two prebiotic/LUCA moments are conditional scenarios.
equation: H_DNA = N_prok × 6×10⁶ bits + N_euk × 1.9×10⁸ bits (2 bits per DNA letter)
cite: Landenmark, H. K. E., Forgan, D. H., & Cockell, C. S. (2015). An estimate of the total DNA in the biosphere. PLoS Biology, 13(6), e1002168. | Giovannoni, S. J., et al. (2005). Genome streamlining in a cosmopolitan oceanic bacterium. Science, 309(5738), 1242–1245.

basis: Installed capacity to store information outside bodies, strictly separated from annual data traffic. Anchored to archaeological stone-tool, tablet and scroll estimates before 500 CE, Buringh and van Zanden's (2009) European manuscript and printed-book series for 500–1844 CE (530 million books printed in 1454–1665, 1.76 billion by 1800, plus East Asian woodblock and Islamic paper libraries), Hilbert and López (2011) for analog film, tape, print and digital storage through 2007 (54.5 exabytes = 4.4×10²⁰ bits in 2000; 295 exabytes = 2.4×10²¹ bits in 2007), and IDC Global StorageSphere installed capacity for 2010–2026 (0.7 zettabytes in 2010, 6.7 zettabytes in 2020, 15 zettabytes = 1.2×10²³ bits today).
equation: M_outside = installed storage of each era (marks, tablets, books, film, disks); today 15 zettabytes
cite: Buringh, E., & van Zanden, J. L. (2009). Charting the 'Rise of the West': Manuscripts and printed books in Europe, a long-term perspective from the sixth to eighteenth centuries. The Journal of Economic History, 69(2), 409–445. | Hilbert, M., & López, P. (2011). The world's technological capacity to store, communicate, and compute information. Science, 332(6025), 60–65. | Rydning, J. (2021, 2025). Worldwide Global StorageSphere Forecast. IDC.

basis: Short-lived state per cell and per neuron, plus installed DRAM.
equation: M_active = 100 bits × N_prok + 1,000 × N_euk + 500 × N_neurons + computer memory (DRAM)

basis: Anchored at every moment to published colony, archaeological or demographic records: microbial mats (10⁸–10¹⁰ cells, Flemming & Wuertz 2019), coral and fish collectives, eusocial Macrotermes and Atta leafcutter ant megacolonies (5–8 million workers, Hölldobler & Wilson 2009), Neolithic villages and Early Dynastic Egypt/Uruk (~0.5–1 million), Achaemenid Persia (~30 million, Taagepera 1979), the 2 CE Han census (57.7 million, Hanshu) and Roman peak (~60 million, Scheidel 2007), Song, Ming and Qing household registers (Ho 1959), and since 1890 the submarine-cable, radio and Internet-linked world human population from HYDE 3.3 and the UN World Population Prospects (8.1 billion). Note two scope shifts in the series: single cells before 555 million years ago, largest animal colony up to 45,000 years ago, largest human settlement or state from 8000 BCE to 1844 CE, and world human population from 1890 onward.
equation: N_group = largest group acting as one (from colony, state and world censuses)
cite: Hölldobler, B., & Wilson, E. O. (2009). The Superorganisms. W. W. Norton. | Scheidel, W. (2007). Demography. In The Cambridge Economic History of the Greco-Roman World (pp. 38–86). Cambridge University Press. | Taagepera, R. (1978, 1979). Size and duration of empires. Social Science Research / Social Science History. | United Nations (2024). World Population Prospects 2024.

basis: Instantaneous cellular respiration inside living cells: 14.0 TW in microbes (0.69 TW deep crust and seabed, 3.89 TW starved soil and dark ocean, 9.42 TW sunlit surface), 48.5 TW in active plant leaves, roots, fungi and protists, and 2.5 TW in animals, summing to 65.0 TW. Measured top down, global net primary production stores about 130 TW (~105 Gt carbon a year; gross photosynthesis ~220–250 TW, Field et al. 1998): the other ~65 TW is chemical bond energy locked each year into dead structural wood, bark, soil humus and peat or released abiotically in wildfires rather than respired as live intracellular metabolic work.
equation: P_bio = P_microbes + P_other cells + P_animals
cite: Field, C. B., Behrenfeld, M. J., Randerson, J. T., & Falkowski, P. (1998). Primary production of the biosphere: integrating terrestrial and oceanic components. Science, 281(5374), 237–240. | Makarieva, A. M., et al. (2008). Mean mass-specific metabolic rates are strikingly similar across life's major domains. PNAS, 105(44), 16994–16999.

basis: Extrasomatic primary energy controlled by hominins and human industry (excluding human food and draft-animal fodder, which belong to biological metabolism). Zero before habitual fire (~1.5 million years ago, Gowlett 2016); Paleolithic to 1665 CE from population (HYDE 3.3) times per-person fuelwood and charcoal use (Smil 2017: rising from 0.28 TW in 1450 and 0.36 TW in 1665 toward 0.65 TW in 1800, correcting earlier socio-metabolic totals that double-counted food and fodder); and 1844–2026 directly from Our World in Data's global primary energy series combining Smil (2017) and the Energy Institute Statistical Review (0.86 TW in 1844, 1.22 TW in 1890, 2.88 TW in 1945, 5.79 TW in 1965, 13.5 TW in 2000, 19.5 TW today).
equation: P_tech = extrasomatic primary energy people use (fire, fuel, electricity), from HYDE × Smil and OWID / Energy Institute
cite: Smil, V. (2017). Energy Transitions: Global and National Perspectives (2nd ed.). Praeger. | Energy Institute (2024, 2025). Statistical Review of World Energy (620 EJ in 2023 ≈ 19.65 TW). | Klein Goldewijk, K., et al. (2017). Anthropogenic land use estimates for the Holocene – HYDE 3.2. Earth System Science Data, 9, 927–953. | Gowlett, J. A. J. (2016). The discovery of fire by humans: a long and convoluted process. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 371, 20150164.

basis: Today's 550 Gt carbon is the measured world total (77.5 Gt microbes, 380 Gt dead wood, 90.5 Gt active plant, fungal and protist tissue, 2.0 Gt animals; Bar-On et al. 2018), and the Early Holocene forest peak (780 Gt) is anchored below Erb et al.'s (2018) zero-land-use potential benchmark. Deep-time moments are set by hand as geological scenarios; no fossil global biomass census exists.
equation: B = B_prok + B_wood + B_euk + B_animal

basis: A model assumption with published bounds for its shares. The 85% for microbes matches bacterial and archaeal genomes, which are about 85–90% coding genes (Koonin & Wolf 2008). The 15% for complex cells sits between humans (about 8% under purifying selection, Rands et al. 2014) and yeast, flies and worms (18–68%, Siepel et al. 2005). The constrained share across wild algae and land plants, which hold most nucleated cells, is not directly measured.
equation: H_sel = 0.85 × microbial DNA bits + 0.15 × other DNA bits
cite: Koonin, E. V., & Wolf, Y. I. (2008). Genomics of bacteria and archaea. Nucleic Acids Research, 36(21), 6688–6719. | Rands, C. M., et al. (2014). 8.2% of the human genome is constrained. PLoS Genetics, 10(7), e1004525. | Siepel, A., et al. (2005). Evolutionarily conserved elements in vertebrate, insect, worm, and yeast genomes. Genome Research, 15(8), 1034–1050.

basis: Set by hand, anchored today against global metagenomic catalogues. About 303 million distinct microbial genes have already been sequenced (Coelho et al. 2022), giving a sampled lower bound near 6×10¹¹ bits, and LUCA at 3.8–4.1 billion years ago is anchored to ~2,600 protein families (Moody et al. 2024). Today's 3.8×10¹² bits implies about 1.9 billion distinct gene clusters globally, six times the sampled catalogue. Intermediate deep-time values are order-of-magnitude estimates with no fossil pangenome source.
equation: H_unique = distinct gene families × bits per family (set by hand)
cite: Coelho, L. P., et al. (2022). Towards the biogeography of prokaryotic genes. Nature, 601, 252–256. | Locey, K. J., & Lennon, J. T. (2016). Scaling laws predict global microbial diversity. PNAS, 113(21), 5970–5975.

basis: Long-term memory adds three stores: DNA, synapses (4.7 bits each, from spine sizes) and outside memory.
equation: M_kept = H_DNA + 4.7 bits × synapses + M_outside

basis: Animal power scales with animal biomass: 2 Gt carbon of animals today (from Bar-On et al. 2018) are assumed to respire 2.5 TW (~1–2 W per kilogram of wet animal mass). No dedicated global empirical inventory of all animal respiration has been compiled; the 2.5 TW conversion is a model assumption.
equation: P_animals = (B_animal ÷ 2 Gt carbon) × 2.5 TW
cite: Makarieva, A. M., et al. (2008). Mean mass-specific metabolic rates are strikingly similar across life's major domains. PNAS, 105(44), 16994–16999.

basis: Total planetary power adds living intracellular respiration (65.0 TW today) and extrasomatic human technological primary power (19.5 TW today) to close at 84.5 TW without double-counting food or draft-animal fodder.
equation: P = P_bio + P_tech

basis: Electricity used by computers and data centres; today 80 GW from data-centre and client device electricity estimates. Pre-2020 values are order-of-magnitude estimates.
equation: P_computers = electricity used by chips and data centres (set by hand per era)
cite: Shehabi, A., et al. (2024). 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

basis: Electrical signals in plants, fungi, microbes and nerveless animals, set by hand. Vascular trees alone give 3×10²⁰ to 3×10²¹ signals a second (Crowther et al. 2015). Potassium waves in bacterial biofilms could add 10²⁴ to 10²⁶ (Prindle et al. 2015), so today's 7×10²³ sits inside the plausible range depending on active biofilm share; earlier moments are unmeasured estimates.
equation: C_electric = cells that signal electrically × signals per cell per second (set by hand)
cite: Prindle, A., et al. (2015). Ion channels enable electrical communication in bacterial communities. Nature, 527, 59–63.

basis: How far the most capable single thinker sits above a typical cell, in digits.
equation: R = log₁₀(C_max ÷ 1,000 signals a second)

basis: A model assumption: actively repaired DNA survives as long as its lineage, set to 50 million years for modern lineages (separated from the 521-year post-mortem half-life of unpowered bone DNA in Allentoft et al. 2012). Fossil surveys give about 11 million years for an average marine species and 28 million for a genus (mean; median 11 million, Raup 1978), while core housekeeping genes last billions of years, so the taxonomic level chosen sets the answer.
equation: Φ = H_DNA × lineage lifetime in years
cite: Raup, D. M. (1978). Cohort analysis of generic survivorship. Paleobiology, 4(1), 1–15.

basis: Set by hand and now checked moment by moment against published reconstructions and thermometer records: Judd and colleagues (2024) for the past 485 million years, Scotese and colleagues (2021) back to 540 million years ago, Snyder (2016), Kaufman and colleagues (2020) and PAGES 2k (2019) across the ice ages and Common Era, and HadCRUT5 and NASA GISTEMP since 1850, with Catling and Zahnle (2020) bounds in the Archean (leaving 2.45 billion to 555 million years ago outside dataset coverage). Eighteen of the 58 covered moments sit outside the primary series' uncertainty range—ten where hand-set values follow the cooler Scotese curve or split the difference with the warmer 2024 assimilation, three in the Hadean and Archean above 0–50 °C carbon-cycle bounds, one for the brief asteroid-winter freeze 66 million years ago, plus 375 million years ago (typed 7–11 °C too cool) and 0.3–0.4 °C offsets at 1000, 1890 and 1965 CE.
equation: T = global mean surface temperature (set by hand, checked against reconstructions and thermometers)
cite: Scotese, C. R., Song, H., Mills, B. J. W., & van der Meer, D. G. (2021). Phanerozoic paleotemperatures: the earth's changing climate during the last 540 million years. Earth-Science Reviews, 215, 103503. | Judd, E. J., et al. (2024). A 485-million-year history of Earth's surface temperature. Science, 385, eadk3705. | Snyder, C. W. (2016). Evolution of global temperature over the past two million years. Nature, 538, 226–228. | Kaufman, D., et al. (2020). Holocene global mean surface temperature, a multi-method reconstruction approach. Scientific Data, 7, 201. | PAGES 2k Consortium (2019). Consistent multidecadal variability in global temperature reconstructions and simulations over the Common Era. Nature Geoscience, 12, 643–649. | Morice, C. P., et al. (2021). An updated assessment of near-surface temperature change from 1850: the HadCRUT5 data set. JGR Atmospheres, 126, e2019JD032361. | Catling, D. C., & Zahnle, K. J. (2020). The Archean atmosphere. Science Advances, 6, eaax1420.

basis: Set by hand and now checked moment by moment against modern dry-air and ice-core measurements (20.95% since 3.3 million years ago; Stolper and colleagues 2016), the Krause and colleagues (2022) biogeochemical reconstruction and wildfire bounds back to 1.5 billion years ago, and Lyons, Reinhard and Planavsky (2014) geochemical bounds before that. Fourteen of the 68 moments fall outside those published bounds: 2.9 billion years ago (typed ten times above the sulfur-isotope ceiling), 635 million years ago (where 3.5% of today's oxygen was typed as 3.5% of the air), nine Ediacaran to Early Devonian moments set above pre-forest oxygen limits, 320 million years ago (placed at the 33% coal-swamp peak roughly 20 million years early), and the end-Permian and Early Triassic crises (typed at 12–14%, below the 15% wildfire floor).
equation: O₂ = share of oxygen in the air (set by hand, checked against reconstructions and ice cores)
cite: Lyons, T. W., Reinhard, C. T., & Planavsky, N. J. (2014). The rise of oxygen in Earth's early ocean and atmosphere. Nature, 506, 307–315. | Krause, A. J., Mills, B. J. W., Merdith, A. S., Lenton, T. M., & Poulton, S. W. (2022). Extreme variability in atmospheric oxygen levels in the late Precambrian. Science Advances, 8, eabm8191. | Stolper, D. A., Bender, M. L., Dreyfus, G. B., Yan, Y., & Higgins, J. A. (2016). A Pleistocene ice core record of atmospheric O₂ concentrations. Science, 353(6306), 1427–1430.

basis: Set by hand and now checked moment by moment against Mauna Loa measurements since 1965, the 800,000-year Antarctic ice-core composite of Bereiter and colleagues (2015), the 420-million-year proxy compilation of Foster, Royer and Lunt (2017) cross-checked against the 2023 Cenozoic synthesis, and Catling and Zahnle (2020) bounds in the Archean (with 2.45 billion to 425 million years ago beyond the Foster compilation). Twenty-eight of the 51 covered moments sit outside the primary series' 95% range, led by brief volcanic and impact spikes smoothed out at half-million-year resolution (251.9, 201 and 66 million years ago), Mesozoic values typed 600–1,200 parts per million above the Foster curve, Paleocene–Eocene values that match the 2023 Cenozoic revision, four Pleistocene moments typed 21–57 parts per million too low (including the warm interglacial 400,000 years ago), and small rounding offsets in the last 5,000 years.
equation: CO₂ = carbon dioxide in the air, parts per million (set by hand, checked against ice cores and proxies)
cite: Foster, G. L., Royer, D. L., & Lunt, D. J. (2017). Future climate forcing potentially without precedent in the last 420 million years. Nature Communications, 8, 14845. | The CenCO2PIP Consortium (2023). Toward a Cenozoic history of atmospheric CO₂. Science, 382, eadi5177. | Bereiter, B., et al. (2015). Revision of the EPICA Dome C CO₂ record from 800 to 600 kyr before present. Geophysical Research Letters, 42(2), 542–549. | NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory (2026). Trends in Atmospheric Carbon Dioxide (Mauna Loa, Hawaii).
